name: Mars-500, SIRIUS and CHAPEA
operator: Institute of Biomedical Problems, Moscow, with ESA, China and NASA
short_status: Completed: six men sealed into chambers in Moscow for 520 days, 3 June 2010 to 4 November 2011. The line runs on through Russia's SIRIUS series to NASA's CHAPEA, whose second crew is due out on 31 October 2026.

facts.label: What Mars-500 was
facts.value: A ground isolation experiment run by the Institute of Biomedical Problems of the Russian Academy of Sciences (IMBP RAN, in Russian ИМБП РАН) in Moscow, with the European Space Agency as the main international partner and Chinese participation. Six men lived in a linked set of sealed chambers and flew a Mars mission that existed only as a schedule, a script and a communications delay. ESA describes the crew as three Russian, two European and one Chinese.

facts.label: Three stages, not one
facts.value: A 14-day shakedown of the chambers in November 2007 with six Russian volunteers, to test the modules and whether people could stand them. A 105-day run from 31 March to 14 July 2009 with an international crew. Then the 520-day run from 3 June 2010 to 4 November 2011. The 520 days is the number everyone quotes, but the programme is all three, and the name Mars-500 covers the whole thing.

facts.label: The facility
facts.value: The NEK ground experimental complex at IMBP (in Russian НЭК), built as linked modules: EU-150 at 150 cubic metres as the crew habitat with individual cabins, EU-100 at 100 cubic metres for medical and psychological work, EU-250 at 250 cubic metres for stores, greenhouse, gym and waste, EU-50 at 50 cubic metres as the landing module, and alongside them a hall of about 1,200 cubic metres dressed as the surface of Mars. Russian sources date the complex's design to 1964 to 1970 and its operation to 1971. Basner and colleagues, writing in PLoS One, give the sealed volume the crew actually lived in as 550 cubic metres, which is the sum of the four numbered modules: for six men and seventeen months, roughly the interior of a large house with no window that shows anything real.

facts.label: The 520-day crew
facts.value: Alexey Sitev commanding, with Sukhrob Kamolov and Alexandr Smoleevskiy, all selected in Russia; Romain Charles of France; Diego Urbina, whom ESA lists as Italian and Colombian and who lived in Turin; and Wang Yue (王跃) of China. All six came out on 4 November 2011. Transliterations vary in the sources, so Sitev also appears as Siteyev or Sitiev and Smoleevskiy as Smoleevsky.

facts.label: The delay
facts.value: ESA states that a 20 minute delay was built into communications with the control centre to simulate an interplanetary mission. A question and its answer therefore stood up to forty minutes apart. That single design decision is what converts mission control from a conversation into correspondence, and it turns out to be the most consequential thing the chambers reproduced.

facts.label: The simulated landing
facts.value: In February 2011 the complex was reconfigured for arrival. ESA records that the crew split into two groups of three with the hatch closed between the modules, one group transferring into the landing module and then, in suits, into the surface hall. Russian sources date the three simulated Marswalks to 14, 18 and 22 February 2011.

facts.label: ESA's science programme
facts.value: ESA ran 13 scientific protocols inside the experiment: adaptation and group dynamics; psychological and cardiac functioning; physical fitness by vibration exercise on a Galileo 2000; spacecraft control training; stress and immunity; blue-enhanced lighting and circadian rhythms; group dynamics and loneliness; physical activity and the serotonergic system; omega-3 supplementation; personal values and group compatibility; retention of medical skills; microbial ecology; and cognitive and emotional adaptation.

facts.label: What it could not simulate
facts.value: No weightlessness, no radiation, no launch, no vacuum on the far side of the wall, and above all no irreversibility. Any of the six could have opened the door, and doctors were on the other side of it. Everything Mars-500 could test was behavioural, psychological and operational, plus the physiology of sleep and activity. That is a real limit on what the results mean, and it is also the point: these are the things no spacecraft design can fix for you.

facts.label: Finding: people quietly wind down
facts.value: Basner and colleagues, in PNAS on 7 January 2013, tracked the crew with wrist actigraphy throughout. Across the mission sleep rose 8.4 per cent, equivalent to 0.59 hours more sleep per crewmember per day. Active wakefulness fell 7.0 per cent, equivalent to 1.12 hours less active waking per day. Rest, meaning awake but sedentary, rose 50.4 per cent, equivalent to 0.54 hours more per day. All three at P less than 0.0001. The authors call it protracted hypokinesis.

facts.label: Finding: four of the six had a problem
facts.value: The same paper reports that a majority, four of six, experienced one or more of: disrupted sleep and wake periodicity (one crewmember), increased displacement of sleep into the diurnal period (two), performance deficits associated with chronic partial sleep deprivation (one), and frequent reductions in perceived sleep quality (two). One crewmember's sleep and wake period varied between 24.72 and 25.06 hours, increased with time in mission and averaged 24.98 hours over the whole 520 days, so that he slid steadily out of phase with the other five.

facts.label: Finding: and two of the six had none
facts.value: Basner and colleagues, in PLoS One on 27 March 2014, report the behavioural half. The crewmember with the highest average mood disturbance score reported symptoms of depression in 93 per cent of mission weeks, reaching mild to moderate levels in more than 10 per cent of them. Two crewmembers, the two with the highest ratings of stress and physical exhaustion, accounted for 85 per cent of all perceived conflicts. And two crewmembers showed neither behavioural disturbances nor reports of psychological distress across the entire 17 months. The spread between individuals is the result.

facts.label: Finding: the fight is with the ground
facts.value: The single most useful sentence in the Mars-500 literature: conflicts with mission control were reported five times more often than conflicts among crewmembers, 41 instances against 8. Six men in 550 cubic metres for a year and a half did not, on the whole, fall out with each other. They fell out with the people at the far end of a forty minute round trip.

facts.label: What it cost
facts.value: Russian Wikipedia puts the project cost at about 15 million US dollars. We could not find a primary IMBP or Roscosmos figure to check that against, so it should be read as an estimate in circulation rather than an audited number.

facts.label: SIRIUS, the successor
facts.value: Scientific International Research In a Unique terrestrial Station, which is how NASA expands it; in Russian, Научные международные исследования на уникальной наземной станции. The same NEK chambers, run jointly by IMBP and NASA's Human Research Program. Russian Wikipedia names Oleg Orlov of IMBP and Bill Paloski of NASA HRP as co-directors; the NASA announcement cited here does not name them. NASA's 2017 announcement set out an intended ladder of 17 days, then four months in 2018, eight months in 2019 and twelve months in 2020. The ladder was climbed, but several years behind that schedule.

facts.label: The four SIRIUS runs
facts.value: SIRIUS-17, 7 to 24 November 2017, six crew under Mark Serov and including Anna Kikina, Ilya Rukavishnikov, Elena Luchitskaya (Luchinskaya in some transliterations), Viktor Fetter of Germany and Natalia Lysova. SIRIUS-19, 19 March to 17 July 2019, six crew including two Americans, Allen Mirkadyrov and Reinhold Povilaitis. SIRIUS-21, 4 November 2021 to 3 July 2022, an eight-month run conducted jointly by Roscosmos, NASA and the Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Centre in Dubai. SIRIUS-23, a 366-day run with six volunteers, two men and four women aged 25 to 37; Russian Wikipedia dates its start to 14 November 2023 and we could not confirm the closing date from a source we were able to open.

facts.label: CHAPEA, the American one
facts.value: NASA's Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog, at Johnson Space Center in Houston. Four crew at a time live in a 1,700 square foot 3D-printed habitat under environmental stressors NASA lists as resource limitations, isolation, equipment failure and significant workloads, with simulated spacewalks including virtual reality. NASA states the aim is to characterise the risk of the planned exploration food system design in relation to crew health and performance. Mission 1 ran 25 June 2023 to 6 July 2024 with Kelly Haston, Anca Selariu, Ross Brockwell and Nathan Jones. Mission 2, 378 days with Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, Matthew Montgomery and James Spicer, began on 19 October 2025; NASA's CHAPEA page, consulted on 24 August 2026 and carrying its own last-updated stamp of 14 April 2026, gives 31 October 2026 as the end date and describes the four as living and working inside the habitat. That is an April 2026 statement read in August 2026. Nothing about it is live, so treat the crew's presence today as unconfirmed.

timeline: Six Russian volunteers spend 14 days inside the NEK chambers to prove the modules work and that people can live in them. This is the beginning of Mars-500 and it is almost never mentioned.
The 105-day stage runs with an international crew, the dress rehearsal for the long one.

The hatch closes on six men for 520 days: Alexey Sitev commanding, Sukhrob Kamolov, Alexandr Smoleevskiy, Romain Charles, Diego Urbina and Wang Yue. Every message to and from the control centre now carries a 20 minute delay in each direction.

Simulated arrival. The crew splits into two groups of three with the hatch closed between them, one group transfers into the landing module and then in suits into the 1,200 cubic metre surface hall, and three Marswalks are conducted on 14, 18 and 22 February. The other three sit above them for the duration, which is the loneliest job in any Mars architecture.
The outer hatch opens after 520 days. All six walk out. ESA's account calls the venture better than expected, and the crew meet the press at RIA Novosti in Moscow on 8 November.

Basner and colleagues publish the actigraphy results in PNAS: sleep up 8.4 per cent, active waking down 7.0 per cent, rest up 50.4 per cent, and four of the six with an identifiable sleep or circadian problem. The companion behavioural paper follows in PLoS One on 27 March 2014.
SIRIUS-17, the first of the successor series, runs 17 days in the same chambers, now jointly with NASA's Human Research Program. Mark Serov commands a crew of six.
SIRIUS-19 runs about four months with two Americans in the crew, and includes a simulated lunar landing rather than a Martian one.
SIRIUS-21, eight months, run jointly by Roscosmos, NASA and the Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Centre in Dubai. It is the last run for which we could confirm a named NASA partnership.
CHAPEA Mission 1 in Houston: Kelly Haston, Anca Selariu, Ross Brockwell and Nathan Jones spend a year in a 3D-printed habitat, with the exploration food system as the primary research question.

SIRIUS-23 begins in Moscow, a 366-day run with six volunteers, two men and four women aged 25 to 37. It is the longest of the SIRIUS series and the first to match Mars-500 in the same order of magnitude.

CHAPEA Mission 2 begins: Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, Matthew Montgomery and James Spicer, 378 days, due out on 31 October 2026. NASA's page, last updated 14 April 2026 and consulted on 24 August 2026, describes them as living and working inside the habitat until that date. No source dated later than April 2026 was found to confirm they are still in.

images.caption: A photograph looking down the length of the NEK hall at the Institute of Biomedical Problems in Moscow, showing the linked pressure modules of the Mars500 facility from outside: a dark red barrel-vaulted module in the foreground, bare metal cylinders behind it ringed with red-painted clamps, walkways and stairs alongside, and a run of sponsor and media boards fixed to the gallery on the right.

The six-man 520-day crew in blue MARS 500 coveralls on the steps outside the modules, photographed by ESA just before they entered the facility at 13:49 local time in Moscow on 3 June 2010, with one man waving.

A man in a green Institute of Biomedical Problems flight suit stands on the access platform in the open outer doorway of the module marked ЭУ 250, arms spread wide, while photographers and staff watch from below; ESA publishes the frame under the title Closing the hatch in June 2010 with a caption describing the 3 June 2010 start of the experiment. ESA does not name the man, so this entry does not either.

The simulated martian terrain hall at IBMP, a dark ribbed room about 10 m by 6 m floored with reddish sand and scattered pale rocks, with pinprick star lights set into the dark walls, a small wheeled rover parked at the back and a figure in a gold-coloured pressure suit carrying an ESA flag on a pole; observers in ordinary clothes stand in the doorway. ESA's own caption calls this training on the simulated terrain, which is a different event from the sealed February 2011 Marswalk, and the room was dressed to resemble the surface at Gusev crater.

A man in a green Institute of Biomedical Problems flight suit stands on the platform and works the handle of the heavy padded door of the ЭУ module, with a doctor in a white coat and another official waiting at the right of frame; ESA's caption reads Opening the door of the Mars500 facility after 520 days.

The four CHAPEA Mission 2 crew, James Spicer, Ross Elder, Matthew Montgomery and Ellen Ellis, standing and sitting in front of a science glovebox inside the 3D-printed Mars Dune Alpha habitat at Johnson Space Center, the printed ribbing of the walls visible behind them and a rainforest print hung on the wall; NASA dates the frame 5 August 2026 and captions it as the crew marking 300 days inside.
